# Statistical model The statistical model can be written as: $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{\textbf{Likelihood and linear predictor}} \\[4pt] \mathbf Y_i &\sim \operatorname{Multinomial}(5,\mathbf p_i) \\[6pt] \mathbf p_i &= \operatorname{Softmax}(\boldsymbol\eta_i) \\[6pt] \boldsymbol\eta_i &= (\eta_{i,-3},\eta_{i,-2},\eta_{i,-1},0, \eta_{i,1},\eta_{i,2},\eta_{i,3})^{\mathsf T} \\[6pt] \eta_{i,k} &= \alpha_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} + \beta_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} \operatorname{mo}_k(\mathrm{t.onset}_i) \\ &+ \beta_{\mathrm{t.day},k}\mathrm{t.day}_i + \beta_{\mathrm{temp},k}\mathrm{temp}_i + \beta_{\mathrm{hum},k}\mathrm{hum}_i + \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum},k} (\mathrm{temp}_i\mathrm{hum}_i) \\[6pt] \alpha_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} &= \bar{\alpha}_{\mathrm{sex}[i],k} + v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{sex}[i],k} \\[6pt] \beta_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} &= \bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{t.onset},k} + v_{\mathrm{condition}[i],\mathrm{t.onset},k} \\[6pt] \operatorname{mo}_k(\mathrm{t.onset}_i) &= (D-1)\sum_{d=1}^{D-1} \zeta_{k,d}\mathbb I(\mathrm{t.onset}_i>d) \\[12pt] &\text{\textbf{Multilevel structure: non-centred parameterisation}} \\[4pt] \mathbf v_j &= \left( v_{j,\mathrm{male},-3}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},-3}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},-3}, \ldots, v_{j,\mathrm{male},+3}, v_{j,\mathrm{female},+3}, v_{j,\mathrm{t.onset},+3} \right)^{\mathsf T} \\[6pt] \mathbf v_j &= \mathbf D_{\sigma}\mathbf L_{\Omega}\mathbf z_j, \qquad j=1,\ldots,72 \\[6pt] \mathbf D_{\sigma} &= \operatorname{diag}(\sigma_r), \qquad r=1,\ldots,18 \\[12pt] &\text{\textbf{Priors}} \\[4pt] \bar{\alpha}_{s,-3},\bar{\alpha}_{s,3} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-2.69,2), \qquad s\in\{\mathrm{male},\mathrm{female}\} \\ \bar{\alpha}_{s,-2},\bar{\alpha}_{s,2} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1.84,2) \\ \bar{\alpha}_{s,-1},\bar{\alpha}_{s,1} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.89,2) \\[6pt] \bar{\beta}_{\mathrm{t.onset},k} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25) \\[6pt] \boldsymbol\zeta_k &\sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(2,2,2,2), \qquad k\in\mathcal K \\[6pt] \beta_{\mathrm{t.day},k} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.25) \\[6pt] \beta_{\mathrm{temp},k} &\sim \begin{cases} \operatorname{Normal}(-1,0.5), & k<0\\ \operatorname{Normal}(1,0.5), & k>0 \end{cases} \\[6pt] \beta_{\mathrm{hum},k} &\sim \begin{cases} \operatorname{Normal}(-0.5,0.25), & k<0\\ \operatorname{Normal}(0.5,0.25), & k>0 \end{cases} \\[6pt] \beta_{\mathrm{temp.hum},k} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0,0.2) \\[6pt] \mathbf z_j &\sim \operatorname{MVN}(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I_{18}), \qquad j=1,\ldots,72 \\[12pt] &\text{\textbf{Hyperpriors}} \\[4pt] \sigma_r &\sim \operatorname{Exponential}(1), \qquad r=1,\ldots,18 \\[6pt] \mathbf L_{\Omega} &\sim \operatorname{LKJ-Cholesky}(2) \end{aligned} $$ {#eq-complete-model} where $$ \begin{gathered} \mathcal K=\{-3,-2,-1,+1,+2,+3\},\qquad D=5,\qquad \zeta_{k,d}\geq0,\qquad \sum_{d=1}^{D-1}\zeta_{k,d}=1 \end{gathered} $$ ## Sex-specific intercepts The model in @eq-complete-model is simplified to a model with a only-intercept model. Specifically: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf Y_i &\sim \operatorname{Multinomial}(5,\mathbf p_i) \\[6pt] \mathbf p_i &= \operatorname{Softmax}(\boldsymbol\eta_i) \\[6pt] \boldsymbol\eta_i &= (\eta_{i,-3},\eta_{i,-2},\eta_{i,-1},0, \eta_{i,1},\eta_{i,2},\eta_{i,3})^{\mathsf T} \\[6pt] \eta_{i,k} &= \alpha_{k} \end{aligned} $$ ::: {.cell} ::: The model in `brms` can be written as ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod.00 <- brm(formula = formula_mod.00, data = nevins_analysis, family = multinomial(refcat = 'y4', link = logit), iter = 4000, warmup = 1000, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 2026 ) ``` ::: where `formula_mod.00` is equal to ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} formula_mod.00 <- bf(vote | trials(5) ~ 1) ``` ::: We can exact the default prior from the model with the function `get_prior()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} get_prior(formula = formula_mod.00, data = nevins_analysis, family = multinomial(refcat = 'y4', link = logit)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` prior class coef group resp dpar nlpar lb ub tag source student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy1 default student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy2 default student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy3 default student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy5 default student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy6 default student_t(3, 0, 2.5) Intercept muy7 default ``` ::: ::: To better understand the implications of this default prior, let's plot it. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom layout-nrow="1" layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Plot for Student's t(3, 0, 2.5) and Normal(0, 4) prior.](prior-predictive-checks_files/figure-html/fig-student-1.png){#fig-student fig-align='center' width=3600} ::: ::: The distribution in @fig-student depicts the log odds of being in category $k$ compared to the reference category '4 - comfortable.' A negative value means that the log odds of falling into the category $k$ relative to '4 - comfortable' will decrease, while a positive value indicates that they will increase. In @fig-student, the left and right dashed lines demarcate tail regions that, with respect to the reference category, can be thought of as 'never' and 'always,' respectively. For instance, log odds of minus five or lower are so extreme that observing a category $k$ compared to the reference category '4 - comfortable' is rendered nearly impossible. The default prior implies that there is \~7\.0% probability of this to happen (with a total of \~13\.9% probability of being lower than $-5$ and higher than $5$). `brms` chooses the prior to moderately regularise the posterior by making it unlikely that the prior biases the inference. However, it is always better to provide specific priors motivated by domain knowledge about the problem at hand. In our case, the response variable (TSV) is theoretically composed of ordered categories. Consequently, we would expect to find an ordering also the intercepts. However, the ordering would depend on the reference category selected and the intercept interpretation. Generally, the intercept represents the predicted thermal sensation vote, where all predictors are set to zero. Although we did not add any predictors yet, we could assume we did. In this scenario, the intercept is the predicted thermal sensation vote for individuals exposed to an indoor air temperature of 0 °C and relative humidity of 0 %. This is a not meaningful scenario where the interpretation of the intercept is an obviously inappropriate extrapolation. There is an easy fix to this situation: we could imagine to centre the predictors. This could be done by (i) subtracting the mean of the data or (ii) using a conventional centring point. We opted for the second option. Specifically, we decided to subtract 25.5 °C from air temperature and 50 % from relative humidity. We chose these values because they correspond to a PMV $\approx$ 0.00, assuming mean radiant temperature of 25.5 °C, airspeed of 0.1 m/s, relative, metabolic rate of 1 met, and clothing level of 0.6 clo. In this context, the intercept represents the predicted thermal sensation vote with indoor air temperature of 25.5 °C and relative humidity of 50 %. As previously mentioned, the reference category is '4 – comfortable.' Assuming that the conditions selected (i.e., air temperature of 25.5 °C and relative humidity of 50 %) correspond to the highest probabilities of observing '4 – comfortable,' we will expect the value of all the log odds for the $k$ categories to be negative but different in magnitude. Specifically, we would expect $|\alpha_{1}|\geq|\alpha_{2}|\geq|\alpha_{3}|\geq 0$ and $|\alpha_{7}|\geq|\alpha_{6}|\geq|\alpha_{5}|\geq 0$. However, there is uncertainty as we are not sure that the defined conditions correspond to the highest probability for the reference category '4 – comfortable.' Luckily, we can encode our expectation and uncertainty in the prior. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Priors for intercepts parameters.](prior-predictive-checks_files/figure-html/fig-new-prior-1.png){#fig-new-prior fig-align='center' width=4500} ::: ::: @fig-new-prior illustrates the prior probability for the six intercepts where $$ \begin{aligned} \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{7} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-2.69, 2)\\ \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{6} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-1.84, 2)\\ \alpha_{3}, \alpha_{5} &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(-0.89, 2)\\ \end{aligned} $$ For example, $\alpha_{1}$ (i.e., '1 – cold') is centred at $-2.69$, encoding our expectation that given the chosen conditions (i.e., air temperature of 25.5 °C and relative humidity of 50 %) and the reference category (i.e., '4 – comfortable'), the intercept should be negative. However, since we are not sure about its magnitude, a standard deviation of $2$ allows this intercept to assume different values but only \~8\.9% probability to be greater than zero. If we now consider $\alpha_{3}$ (i.e., '3 – slightly cool'), we still expect the log odds to be negative but we also allow for a \~17\.9% probability to be positive (i.e., greater than zero). Since the category '3 – slightly cool' is adjacent to the reference category '4 – comfortable', we assume that it is much more likely that the chosen conditions are perceived as 'slightly cool' (i.e., \~17\.9%) rather than 'cold' (i.e, \~8\.9%). Additionally, we implicitly assume that the intercepts are symmetric (around the reference category), but this is only an initial, convenient choice, and given the data, the posterior for the intercepts can be different. To evaluate the practical implication of the priors, we can perform a prior predictive check. We can do this by simulating a sample of 500 data points from the prior distribution for each parameter $\mu$ and then input it in the softmax function. The result of this simulation is visualised in the following figure. ::: {.cell .fig-cap-location-bottom layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Prior predictve check for 1,000 sampled data points (black dots are the means and black lines the 95% credible intervals).](prior-predictive-checks_files/figure-html/fig-ppcheck-sample-1.png){#fig-ppcheck-sample fig-align='center' width=6300} ::: ::: ## The model in @eq-complete-model is simplified to a model with a sex-specific intercepts. Specifically: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf Y_i &\sim \operatorname{Multinomial}(5,\mathbf p_i) \\[6pt] \mathbf p_i &= \operatorname{Softmax}(\boldsymbol\eta_i) \\[6pt] \boldsymbol\eta_i &= (\eta_{i,-3},\eta_{i,-2},\eta_{i,-1},0, \eta_{i,1},\eta_{i,2},\eta_{i,3})^{\mathsf T} \\[6pt] \eta_{i,k} &= \bar{\alpha}_{\mathrm{sex}[i],k} \end{aligned} $$ ## Condition-varying intercepts ## Monotonic time-onset component ## Condition-varying time-onset coefficients ## Correlation between condition-varying parameters ## Temperature ## Relative humidity ## Temperature × relative humidity interaction ## Time of day
